facts.statement: The genus Edaphodon was first described by William Buckland in 1838.
The type species of the genus is Edaphodon bucklandii.
Edaphodon is classified as a genus in the family Callorhinchidae, though it is sometimes assigned to the family Edaphodontidae.
facts.quote: Edaphodon was a fish genus of the family Callorhinchidae (sometimes assigned to Edaphodontidae).

facts.statement: Edaphodon was a member of the order Chimaeriformes, a group of cartilaginous fish related to sharks and rays.
facts.quote: As a member of the Chimaeriformes, Edaphodon was a type of rabbitfish, a cartilaginous fish related to sharks and rays.

facts.statement: Edaphodon first appeared in the Aptian age of the Lower Cretaceous and went extinct during the Pliocene.
facts.quote: The genus appeared in the Aptian age of the Lower Cretaceous and vanished in the Pliocene.

facts.statement: The genus was most prominent during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: It was most prominent during the Late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Edaphodon species were found in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, including New Zealand and Antarctica.
facts.quote: Many Edaphodon species were found in the Northern Hemisphere, but species from the Southern Hemisphere are also known (e.g., E. kawai from New Zealand and E. snowhillensis from Antarctica).

facts.statement: Edaphodon fed using six pairs of tooth plates bearing hypermineralized areas called tritors, located on the lower jaw and two upper jaw plates.
facts.quote: Like other chimaeriforms, it fed using six pairs of tooth plates—one pair on the lower jaw (mandibular) and two pairs on the upper (vomerine and palatine), which bear tooth-like hypermineralized areas known as tritors.

facts.statement: Edaphodon's tooth plates had distinct patterns: vomerine plates had rod-like tritors, palatine plates had one large outer tritor with pads in the center, and mandibular plates had a beak-like tritor with pads at the edges and center.
facts.quote: In Edaphodon, the vomerine tooth plates are covered in rod-like tritors; each palatine tooth plate is massive, and has one large tritor on the outer edge and two large tritor pads and one small tritor pad in the middle; and each mandibular tooth plate is massive and has a beak-like tritor at the front end, along with two pairs of tritor pads at their outer edges and a single large tritor pad in the middle.

facts.statement: Edaphodon likely used its tritors to crush hard-shelled prey and slice fish, sharks, and marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Edaphodon would have used its tritors for both crushing hard-shelled and slicing other prey such as fishes, sharks, and marine reptiles.

facts.statement: The largest mandibular tooth plates of E. sedgwickii reached 225 mm, while those of E. snowhillensis reached 180 mm.
facts.quote: the largest E. sedgwickii mandibular tooth plates reach 225 mm, and E. snowhillensis mandibular tooth plates also reached 180 mm.

facts.statement: Some species of Edaphodon, such as E. mirificus, reached lengths of over 3 meters, with one individual estimated at 3.43 meters.
facts.quote: Based on this calculation, the species E. barberi, E. mirificus, and E. snowhillensis have been estimated at over 3 m in length, with one individual of E. mirificus reaching 3.43 m.

facts.statement: The parent group for the genus Edaphodon is the family Edaphodontidae.
Edaphodon belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, which includes cartilaginous fish.
Edaphodon lived from the Aptian to the Zanclean stages, spanning from 119.57 to 3.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Zanclean (119.57 to 3.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 65 recorded fossil occurrences of Edaphodon in the Paleobiology Database.
